beforePage.section: Growing Techniques · Planning a new plot
beforePage.title: Beds and paths
beforePage.subtitle: that work for you
beforePage.lead: A vegetable garden does not have to look like a little farm. Permanent paths let you work the crops without repeatedly walking over, compacting and then loosening the same soil.
beforePage.diagramTitle: A finger layout saves growing space
beforePage.diagramCaption: Paths stop short where every part of the remaining bed can still be reached. This is a layout idea, not a scale plan.

blocks.title: Keep the middle within reach
blocks.text: About {bedWidth} is a useful starting width for a bed reached from both sides, but your arms decide the final measurement. Make a bed against a wall narrower. Peg out paths wide enough to work from, move a barrow and turn comfortably; try the layout before committing yourself.

blocks.title: Borrow a leaf’s design
blocks.text: Leaf veins branch off a main route instead of crossing the whole leaf. My allotment paths work much the same way: fingers of access stop before the far edge, leaving extra growing ground. The trade-off is an occasional longer walk round. Use through-paths wherever access matters more.

blocks.title: Work with sun and slope
blocks.text: Where the site allows, I run long beds north to south so tall crops share their shade across the day. Existing buildings and drainage may matter more than compass neatness. Keep tall crops from shading the whole plot, and give rain a route away from low spots.

closing.title: Sides are optional
closing.text: Mounded beds need no timber and leave fewer crevices for slugs in my wet garden. Framed beds hold a flatter surface and can raise the working height. Choose what makes the plot easier to use, then keep your feet on the paths. Prepare the ground using the Cultivation pages.

beforePage.source: John: Raised Beds, including leaf-vein layouts; Sun, Drainage & Access, 00:03–05:37.

beforePage.title: Beds and paths
beforePage.subtitle: continued
beforePage.lead: Give the paths a shape that suits the ground, then try it out with pegs and string. A clever drawing is only useful if you can work from it.
beforePage.imageAlt: Two garden layouts: finger paths stop before the back edge; leaf-like branches stop before the outside edge. Both leave continuous growing soil beyond the path ends.
imageCaptions: Finger paths enter from one side.
A leaf pattern branches from a central path.
bodyParagraphs: I use short paths that stop before the far edge, leaving an extra strip of growing ground. Fingers enter from one side; leaf-like branches spread from a central path, like veins in a leaf.
These shapes can save path space, provided all the soil remains within reach. The compromise is more walking round and less turning room. I like them on my plot; through-paths may suit you better.

blocks.title: Work with sun and slope
blocks.text: Where the site allows, I run long beds north to south so tall crops share their shade across the day. Existing buildings and drainage may matter more than compass neatness. Watch where rain collects before settling the layout.

blocks.title: Try the paths for size
blocks.text: Peg out the edges, then walk the routes with a loaded barrow. Allow room to park, turn and work beside it. Check with everyone who will use the plot; a path that suits you may be awkward for somebody else.

closing.title: Sides are optional
closing.text: Mounded beds need no timber and leave fewer crevices for slugs in my wet garden. Framed beds hold a flatter surface and can raise the working height. Choose what makes the plot easier to use, then prepare the ground using the Cultivation pages.
